founded.what: The year a newly married couple founded the house at Épernay and joined their two names, Perrier and Jouët, by the house's own account.

place: Épernay, Vallée de la Marne, Champagne

kind.means: A négociant manipulant, a house in the trade's own word: it grows Chardonnay of its own in the Côte des Blancs, buys more fruit from growers and makes the wine itself.

story: Perrier-Jouët was founded at Épernay in 1811 by a newly married couple, by the house's own account: Perrier, a cork merchant of the town, and his wife, born Jouët, whose two names the house joined. On the founder's death in 1854 his son took charge. In 1902 the house asked Émile Gallé (1846 to 1904), the Art Nouveau glass master of Nancy, to design a bottle. Gallé enamelled four magnums with a spray of white Japanese anemones, and the flower became the house's emblem. The magnums were found again in the cellars long afterwards, and they inspired Belle Epoque, the prestige cuvée, whose first vintage, the 1964, came in the anemone bottle. By the house's press kit and one history, its first bottles were opened in Paris in 1969, at a party for the seventieth birthday of the jazz composer Duke Ellington, born in 1899. In the United States the wine was long sold as Fleur de Champagne, and merchants date the move to the one name worldwide to 2011. In August 1999 Seagram sold Perrier-Jouët together with Mumm, and in 2005 the house passed to Pernod Ricard with its purchase of Allied Domecq, by the group's own history.

style.line: Delicate and fresh rather than powerful: the house builds its prestige wines on Chardonnay of the Côte des Blancs, and the anemone of 1902 is its emblem.
style.grapes: Chardonnay of the Côte des Blancs is the heart of the prestige wines, from Cramant and Avize above all; Grand Brut leans on Pinot Noir and Meunier, 40 per cent each, by the house.
style.reserve: Up to 15 per cent reserve wines in Grand Brut, by its page; another page of the house gives 12 to 20 per cent.
style.lees: At least three years for the classic cuvées, well beyond the appellation's rule, and at least six for Belle Epoque, by the house.
style.dosage: 8 to 10 grams a litre for Grand Brut; 8 for Belle Epoque 2014 and 2016 and 7 for the 2018, by the house.

nv.name: Grand Brut
nv.note: The non vintage Brut, 40 per cent each Pinot Noir and Meunier with 20 per cent Chardonnay by the house, blended from around fifty crus.

cuvee.name: Belle Epoque

first.what: The first vintage, by the house; its first bottles were opened in Paris in 1969, by the house's press kit and one history.

cuvee.rhythm: A vintage wine since the 1964, made in the years the house declares; its own pages show the 2014, 2016 and 2018 vintages, and a rosé of the 2013.
cuvee.blend: Chardonnay about half, Pinot Noir a little less and a little Meunier, by the house's pages and critics' sheets back to the 2004.
cuvee.sites: For the 2016, by the house: Chardonnay of Cramant, Avize, Chouilly, Le Mesnil-sur-Oger and Vertus in the Côte des Blancs, with Pinot Noir of Mailly on the Montagne de Reims.
cuvee.making: A blend of Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and a little Meunier, aged on its lees in the house's cellars at Épernay for at least six years before disgorging, by the house's page for the 2018. The dosage is set for each vintage: 8 grams a litre for the 2014 and 2016, 7 for the 2018.
cuvee.lees: At least six years, by the house's page for the 2018.
cuvee.bottle: Émile Gallé enamelled four magnums with a spray of white Japanese anemones in 1902; the flower became the house's emblem, and the anemone bottle has dressed Belle Epoque since its first vintage.
cuvee.young: Crisp orchard fruit, freshly baked bread and honeycomb, with warm biscuit on the finish, in a merchant's note of a vintage on release.
cuvee.aged: With time it grows nuttier, with fine, creamy vanilla tones over the delicate fruit of its youth, in a critic's note of the 2000.

forms.name: Belle Epoque Rosé
forms.note: The rosé of a declared year, the 2013 among those the house shows.

forms.name: Belle Epoque Blanc de Blancs
forms.note: The form of the cuvée made from Chardonnay alone.

cuvee.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius, never ice cold; no need to decant; a tulip or a white wine glass rather than a narrow flute.

table.house45: Perrier-Jouët was founded at Épernay in 1811 by a newly married couple, and it joined their two names. In 1902 the Art Nouveau glass master Émile Gallé painted four magnums for the house with white Japanese anemones. The flower became its emblem, and you will see it on the bottle. The style leans on Chardonnay from the Côte des Blancs, delicate rather than powerful. Grand Brut is the non vintage bottle most guests know. Its prestige cuvée is Belle Epoque, first made in the 1964 vintage and sold in that anemone bottle ever since.
table.house10: Perrier-Jouët is the Épernay house of 1811 whose bottles wear the white anemones Émile Gallé painted in 1902.
table.cuvee45: Belle Epoque is the prestige cuvée of Perrier-Jouët, a vintage wine first made in 1964. Chardonnay makes about half of it, from Cramant, Avize and other villages of the Côte des Blancs. Pinot Noir and a little Meunier make up the rest. It rests at least six years in the cellars at Épernay before it is sold. The bottle carries the white Japanese anemones that Émile Gallé painted for the house in 1902. Expect crisp orchard fruit, freshly baked bread and honeycomb. I serve it at 8 to 10 degrees, in a tulip or a white wine glass.
table.sale: If you would like a bottle that tells a story at the table, Belle Epoque wears the white anemones Émile Gallé painted in 1902, with Chardonnay led vintage Champagne inside. May I open one for the table?
table.cuvee10: Belle Epoque is the vintage prestige cuvée of Perrier-Jouët, Chardonnay led, in the bottle painted with white anemones.
table.cuvee20: Belle Epoque is the vintage prestige cuvée of Perrier-Jouët, first made in 1964 and about half Chardonnay. Its bottle carries the white Japanese anemones that Émile Gallé painted for the house in 1902.

guests.q: Is Fleur de Champagne the same wine?
guests.a: Yes. Belle Epoque was long sold in the United States as Fleur de Champagne. It is the same wine, and merchants date the one name worldwide to 2011.

Émile Gallé, the Art Nouveau glass master of Nancy, who enamelled four magnums with white Japanese anemones for the house in 1902. The cuvée itself came more than sixty years later, with the 1964 vintage.

guests.q: Is Belle Epoque a Blanc de Blancs?
guests.a: No. It is about half Chardonnay, with Pinot Noir and a little Meunier. The house also makes Belle Epoque Blanc de Blancs, of Chardonnay alone.
No. It is a Brut, 8 grams a litre for the 2016 and 7 for the 2018 by the house, so dry, with a soft finish.

traps: Belle Epoque is sold as Fleur de Champagne in some markets: it is the same wine.
The painted anemones date from 1902, long before the cuvee itself.
The house prints Belle Epoque with no accent; the class sheet and the library write Belle Époque. It is one wine under one name.
Belle Epoque is Perrier-Jouët's, in the anemone bottle; Palmes d'Or is Nicolas Feuillatte's, in the black faceted bottle, and La Grande Dame is Veuve Clicquot's.

sheet.label: Belle Epoque
sheet.note: The sheet writes Belle Époque with an accent, as French spelling would; the house prints Belle Epoque with none. It is the same wine and the same name, the beautiful era.

questions.q: Which prestige cuvée of the class sheet comes in a bottle painted with white Japanese anemones?
questions.exp: Belle Epoque is Perrier-Jouët's, in the anemone bottle of 1902. La Grande Dame is Veuve Clicquot's, Palmes d'Or is Nicolas Feuillatte's in a black bottle and Cristal is Louis Roederer's in clear glass.

questions.q: In which year was Perrier-Jouët founded at Épernay by a newly married couple?
questions.exp: The house dates itself from 1811. 1743 is the founding of Moët & Chandon, 1902 the year of Gallé's anemones and 1964 the first vintage of Belle Epoque.

questions.q: Which vintage was the first Belle Epoque, the prestige cuvée of Perrier-Jouët?
questions.exp: The first Belle Epoque was the 1964 vintage. 1902 is the year Gallé painted the anemones, 1969 the year its first bottles were opened in Paris, and 1811 the founding of the house.

report: Built on the library's p-perrier-jouet: founded 1811, the anemones of 1902 and the Fleur de Champagne name kept; its two traps are kept word for word, unaccented cuvee included, with a full stop added, because a shared trap must read alike.

Tension: the library and the region record call the house Chardonnay led; Belle Epoque is about half Chardonnay, but the house's Grand Brut is 40 per cent Pinot Noir, 40 Meunier and 20 Chardonnay, so the record calls the prestige wines Chardonnay based and says so of Grand Brut.
The founders are described, not named: neither's dates were found in two sources; the cork trade of the husband and the son's taking charge in 1854 rest on Wikipedia and Difford's Guide.

Émile Gallé's dates, 1846 to 1904, rest on the Musée de l'École de Nancy and Britannica; the plan's release in 1969 is told as the opening of the first bottles at Duke Ellington's seventieth birthday party, by the house's press kit and a World of Fine Wine review, and the house's own history dates the cuvée to 1964 alone.
The head of the house who commissioned Gallé is named on the house's pages, but his dates were not found, so the record says the house asked Gallé.

Ownership: Mumm's majority holding is dated 1950 by Difford's Guide and 1959 by two others, so it is left out; Seagram's sale in August 1999 is Wine Spectator's, and the passage to Pernod Ricard in 2005 with Allied Domecq is the group's own history; the step through Allied Domecq around 2000 or 2001 is left out.
Fleur de Champagne used in the United States until about 2011 rests on two merchants' pages and a label of the 2011 so named; the house's own pages read gave no year.

The blend, about half Chardonnay with 45 per cent Pinot Noir and 5 Meunier, is the house's for the 2018 and Wine.com's and Jancis Robinson's for earlier vintages; the villages are the house's for the 2016, Dizy and Mailly for older ones by Difford's.

The young glass is a merchant's note of the 2012 (Wine.com, its address not returned by the search, so a refuter should confirm it) and the aged glass Decanter's of the 2000; the forms are told only as far as the house's pages named them.
style.vessels and style.malolactic are empty: no page read states either.
kind.code: NM was not read on a label; it is inferred from the house owning Chardonnay vines and buying fruit across around fifty crus, and a refuter should read a label.
The serving temperature is the Codex's reference for sparkling wine; the house's own figure was not found.
